name: Ivan Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, have an MBA, and manage a team of fourteen claims handlers at a large insurer. We review damaged-home claims, assign complex cases, and decide which complaint needs a senior person before it becomes a formal appeal. My pay is high for this job because I run the hardest desk, but the work is still a long string of judgment calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life outside the office like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, who teaches at a college. We have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other management jobs in this city. I sometimes use an approved AI tool to draft a neutral acknowledgement, then read the claim myself; I do not let a draft decide what a family gets paid. We are paying off the apartment loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau is a modest office change. The claims still need careful readers, and no one should lose credit for correcting a bad draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and pay remain secure. The small tool might clear routine letters, leaving more time for disputed water damage cases. I am more concerned about the department quietly raising daily targets than about this mild technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’ll keep reviewing the weekly appeal sample with two handlers. If the small drafting feature arrives, I’ll compare twenty of its letters with our approved wording and bring any errors to the staff meeting. I’ll keep our usual monthly savings transfer; I see no reason to change our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income. The workload could creep up, but I have a voice in how the desk is run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would matter most in a letter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Telling a policyholder that a refusal is final when they still have a right to appeal. That sentence changes whether a person asks for help. I would stop using the draft until the wording is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the team if the tool saved time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I would count the minutes honestly. I would also say which corrections people made. Speed should not erase the work of catching an unfair sentence.

say: **Claims decisions** still need careful readers, even when a tool drafts the routine letters.
I would give handlers **credit** for correcting unfair wording before a policyholder receives it.
think: My **job and pay** look secure under a small drafting change.
I worry about **higher daily targets** more than the tool itself.
do: **Review** the weekly appeal sample with two handlers.
**Compare** twenty drafted letters with approved appeal wording after the feature arrives.
**Continue** the usual monthly transfer into our savings account.
feel: I feel **calm** about income, watchful about workload.
S0.quote: Speed should not erase the work of catching an unfair sentence.
fieldNote: His **nine-month reserve** and many local openings make a mild change manageable.
He measures both **speed and corrections**, keeping attention on the policyholder’s right to appeal.

steps.text: Review the weekly appeal sample with two claims handlers
Compare twenty AI draft letters against approved appeal wording
Continue the household savings transfer each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can draft claims letters, check policies, schedule inspections and answer simple questions. I’d tell management to bargain over targets before those savings become a reason to load more cases on each handler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, those tasks fill much of my desk too. I may keep a role settling difficult appeals, but our fourteen-person team could shrink, and my management post is not protected by a good performance review. My partner’s salary and our savings give us room, though I would hate to see junior staff pushed out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’ll take the company’s paid training on its claims checker if my place is approved, and I’ll test it on closed cases with known appeal outcomes. I’ll ask our staff representative to put case loads and error appeals on the next bargaining agenda. If the unit cuts posts, I’ll look at open appeal-manager jobs across town before accepting a lower title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the team and my own post. I can prepare and have choices, but I cannot set the company’s headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which closed case would you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One claim involved a pipe leak and two separate repair estimates. The first decision missed the second estimate, and the appeal corrected it. I want to know whether the checker sees both documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the staff representative in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One manager’s complaint can be ignored as a personal worry. Agreed measures for appeals and case loads would apply to everyone. I would share the error sample, not just make a speech.

say: **AI claims work** should come with agreed case loads and appeal checks.
I’d ask the staff representative to put **targets** on the bargaining agenda.
think: The fourteen-person team could **shrink**, including my management post.
My partner’s salary and **savings** give options, but junior staff face a harder fall.
do: **Take** paid claims-checker training if my place is approved.
**Share** case-load and appeal evidence with the staff representative.
**Check** open appeal-manager jobs if the unit cuts posts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about headcount, with several options still available.
S1.quote: One manager’s complaint can be ignored as a personal worry.
fieldNote: He uses a **staff representative** to turn personal concern into measured terms for the whole desk.
His own **management risk** remains real despite high pay, a partner’s salary and substantial savings.

steps.text: Take paid claims-checker training if the company approves his place
Give case-load and appeal evidence to the staff representative
Check local appeal-manager vacancies if claims posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do almost any thinking task in our claims office. We should ask for a joint staffing plan and insist that people can challenge a machine’s refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 it could read the policy, price the repair and write the appeal response. Robots capable of hands-on work come around 2031, but my job is on a screen, so that later date does not shelter me. I expect the claims team to contract and think my own post could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d meet the staff representative about a written severance and appeal-rights proposal, and I’d get our monthly spending figures in one place with my partner. In 2027 I’d apply for two open complaint-resolution posts at other insurers if their pay and appeal authority are real. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d take one of those posts only if offered; otherwise I’d use our reserve while seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed by what it could do to claims staff and customers. My own bills are covered for a while, but that does not make the loss small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the joint plan need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dates, severance amounts, paid retraining places and a named person who can overturn an AI refusal. A promise to be fair is not a plan. I would ask the representative to bring the draft to the whole team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-month reserve lets us refuse a bad first offer. We would still cut no essential bills until a cut notice arrives. I would rather make a measured choice than spend the cushion in fear.

say: **AGI by 2028** calls for a joint staffing plan and a human appeal route.
I would ask for **severance figures** before any cuts.
think: Claims thinking work could disappear in **2028**, before hands-on robots around 2031.
I expect **team cuts** and could lose my own post.
do: **Meet** the staff representative about severance and appeal rights next month.
**Apply** in 2027 for complaint-resolution posts if pay and authority are real.
**Use** the nine-month reserve for bills only if my job ends.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own post, and alarmed by likely cuts and weaker appeal rights for claimants.
S2.quote: Our nine-month reserve lets us refuse a bad first offer.
fieldNote: His **own savings** do not erase a realistic risk to his post or concern for claimants.
The **2028 date** is his desk-work exposure; robots around 2031 are a later issue.

steps.text: Meet the staff representative to draft severance and appeal demands
Apply for complaint-resolution vacancies if pay and authority are real

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to build an appeal process people can actually use. I would press for a published rule that a person reviews a disputed refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years may let me move toward complaint investigations while keeping my salary. Thinking AI still arrives in 2031, and robots around 2034 are later; our desk roles do not gain three extra years. I can see a job path, but no one has promised me a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d spend one paid afternoon a month with the internal complaints investigators if my manager approves cover for my desk. I’d take an accredited investigation course only if the employer funds it and gives me work time. After 2031, I’d apply for an investigator lead post if it exists and still lets people reverse a wrong decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I have time to test a real role. I would rather learn the evidence rules than collect a course badge with no opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you observe with the investigators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How they interview a policyholder and decide which photographs count when the paperwork conflicts. I know policy wording, but I have less practice weighing witness accounts. That is the skill gap I want to test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refuses funding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present desk and use a free seminar to understand the basics, but I would not claim to be trained. A formal investigation course is expensive. I would revisit it if an actual paid post appeared.

say: **Five years** could support a human review rule for disputed refusals.
I’d ask for a **published process** before AGI reaches claims.
think: Desk roles face AGI in **2031**; robots around 2034 do not add time for us.
An investigator path is **possible**, but no vacancy is promised.
do: **Shadow** complaints investigators monthly from January 2027 if desk cover is approved.
**Take** an investigation course only with employer funding and paid work time.
**Apply** after 2031 for an investigator lead vacancy with real reversal authority.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test the work and funding.
S3.quote: I would rather learn the evidence rules than collect a course badge with no opening.
fieldNote: His **training plan** depends on funded time and a job that actually handles disputed decisions.
He names a specific **skill gap** in weighing witness accounts rather than assuming his MBA transfers.

steps.text: Shadow complaints investigators monthly if his manager approves desk cover
Take investigation training only with employer funding and paid time
Apply after 2031 for investigator lead only if vacancy allows reversing wrong refusals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to settle appeal rights and retraining terms in public, while people can still see what is coming. The company should not wait until the last two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish paying our home loan and have a larger reserve by then if both salaries hold. My claims-management screen work still faces AGI in 2036; robots around 2039 are a separate issue for adjusters at damaged buildings. I might leave management for investigations sooner if the post is worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep leading the appeals sample and continue our monthly savings transfer. I’d work with the staff representative to seek a written human-review rule, and I’d take a funded investigation placement if a paid opening appears before 2036 with real cases, supervision and no salary cut. In the first year after 2036, I’d move to an investigator job only if its authority and salary suit our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point, but a decade gives us room to bargain and choose. I am not counting on the company keeping my current desk unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the placement worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real case load, a supervisor who can teach me, and no cut in salary during the trial. I would not leave a well-paid post for a ceremonial placement. My partner and I would check the offer together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should set the review rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claimants, staff and the regulator should all be heard. A company cannot write its own appeal rule without anyone testing it. I would bring anonymised examples of errors, with personal details removed.

say: A **decade** allows public appeal rules and written retraining terms.
I would bring **anonymised errors** to the discussion.
think: Both salaries could clear the **home loan** and grow our reserve if they hold.
My desk work faces AGI in **2036**; robots around 2039 affect site adjusters later.
do: **Continue** the weekly appeal sample and monthly savings transfer.
**Work** with the staff representative on a written human-review rule.
**Take** a funded investigation placement if an opening appears without a pay cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but able to bargain and choose over a decade.
S4.quote: A company cannot write its own appeal rule without anyone testing it.
fieldNote: His **collective route** joins claimants, staff and regulator rather than leaving appeal policy to one company.
The **placement** is conditional on real cases, funded supervision and salary protection.

steps.text: Keep reviewing the weekly sample of claims appeals
Continue the monthly household savings transfer
Work with the staff representative on a human-review rule
Take funded investigation placement with real cases and supervision only if salary holds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Claims staff could lose jobs before a fair appeal route is ready, and my own post might be among them. A binding staffing timetable, paid investigation places and a human right to challenge refusals would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the person whose flooded room was refused by an AI whether a fast answer felt fair. I can replace a report. A family cannot replace the month they spent waiting for a proper hearing.

headlineQuote: A family cannot replace the month they spent waiting for a proper hearing.
portrait: **Ivan, 27**, is an MBA-trained claims manager leading fourteen handlers at a large insurer.
His **high pay**, partner’s teaching salary, nine-month reserve and many local openings give him choices.
He uses approved **AI drafting** occasionally but checks claims and appeal rights himself.
He moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to anxiety about his own post by 2028, while pressing for collective terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut claims jobs before a fair human appeal route is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A binding **staffing timetable**, paid investigation places and a right to challenge AI refusals would help.
